meta.provenance: Concepts and trap structures derived from KMF/Gremlin's GRE source set; every stem, all numbers, all options, all explanations and all figures are original. No source text or artwork reproduced. Several questions recast into numeric-entry and multiple-answer form, since the Plane Geometry source pool skews to single-answer MCQ and quantitative comparison.

questions.question: J and K are two distinct points in a plane. Which of the following best describes the set of all points in that plane that are the same distance from J as they are from K?
options: A. The set contains no points
B. The set contains exactly one point
C. The set contains exactly two points
D. The set is a line
E. The set is a circle
questions.explanation: The midpoint of segment JK is one such point, so the set is not empty. Take any point M off the line JK with MJ = MK: triangle JMK is isosceles, and the perpendicular dropped from M to JK lands exactly on the midpoint. Conversely, every point on the line through the midpoint perpendicular to JK is equidistant from J and K, by the two congruent right triangles it creates. So the set is precisely the perpendicular bisector of JK, which is a line.
questions.trap: Students picture only the midpoint and answer 'exactly one point', or they think of 'equal distances from a point' and answer 'a circle'. A circle is the set of points a fixed distance from one centre; here the distances to two different points are being matched, and that produces a straight line.

questions.question: A rectangular hall floor is to be covered completely by square tiles whose sides are 6 inches long. The tiles are laid edge to edge with no gaps, and no tile is cut. If exactly 1,200 tiles are used, which of the following could be the dimensions of the floor? (Note: 12 inches = 1 foot.)
questions.explanation: A tile 6 inches on a side is half a foot on a side, so each tile covers (1/2)(1/2) = 0.25 square foot. Using 1,200 tiles covers 1,200 x 0.25 = 300 square feet. Checking the products: 12 x 20 = 240, 15 x 20 = 300, 15 x 25 = 375, 20 x 20 = 400, and 20 x 30 = 600. Only 15 feet by 20 feet gives 300 square feet, and both 15 and 20 are whole numbers of half-feet, so the tiles fit without cutting.
questions.trap: Students convert the side correctly to 0.5 foot but then use 0.5 square foot as the tile's area, doubling the total to 600 square feet and choosing 20 feet by 30 feet. Halving a length quarters the area, so the conversion factor is 0.25, not 0.5.

questions.question:
The parallel sides of trapezoid WXYZ have lengths XY = 5 and WZ = 13, and the nonparallel sides have lengths WX = 7 and YZ = 9, as shown above. Segment PQ (not shown) is parallel to the two parallel sides, with P on side WX and Q on side YZ. If PQ divides WXYZ into two trapezoids having equal perimeters, what is WP + QZ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="30,180 75,70 171,70 280,180"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="16" y="194">W</text><text x="62" y="62">X</text><text x="170" y="62">Y</text><text x="286" y="194">Z</text><text x="150" y="198">13</text><text x="118" y="60">5</text><text x="36" y="124">7</text><text x="232" y="124">9</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: Let WP + QZ = p. Since P is on WX and Q is on YZ, the remaining pieces satisfy PX + YQ = (7 + 9) - p = 16 - p. The lower trapezoid WPQZ has perimeter WP + PQ + QZ + WZ = p + PQ + 13, and the upper trapezoid PXYQ has perimeter PX + XY + YQ + PQ = (16 - p) + 5 + PQ. Setting these equal, the shared PQ cancels: p + 13 = 21 - p, so 2p = 8 and p = 4.
questions.trap: Students split the nonparallel sides evenly, taking WP + QZ to be half of 7 + 9 = 16, and answer 8, or they halve the difference and answer 2. The cut is not a midline; it is placed so that the two 13-and-5 bases are balanced out, which pushes PQ well below the middle.

questions.question:
In the figure above, square JKLM is inscribed in rectangle ABCD so that J is the midpoint of AB and L is the midpoint of DC. Points P and Q are the midpoints of AD and BC, and K and M lie on segment PQ with PM = KQ = 6. If the area of square JKLM is 98, what is the area of rectangle ABCD?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="30" y="35" width="260" height="140"/><line x1="30" y1="105" x2="290" y2="105" stroke-width="1"/><polygon points="160,35 230,105 160,175 90,105"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="18" y="30">A</text><text x="288" y="30">B</text><text x="288" y="192">C</text><text x="18" y="192">D</text><text x="156" y="28">J</text><text x="234" y="102">K</text><text x="156" y="192">L</text><text x="76" y="102">M</text><text x="16" y="118">P</text><text x="292" y="118">Q</text><text x="55" y="98">6</text><text x="253" y="98">6</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: For a square, area equals half the square of a diagonal, so if the diagonals of JKLM have length d then d^2/2 = 98, giving d^2 = 196 and d = 14. Segment JL is one diagonal; since J and L are the midpoints of the opposite sides AB and DC, JL runs straight across the rectangle and equals the rectangle's height, so AD = 14. The other diagonal KM lies along PQ and also has length 14, so the rectangle's width is PM + MK + KQ = 6 + 14 + 6 = 26. The area is 14 x 26 = 364.
questions.trap: Students drop the two 6-unit pieces and answer 14 x 14 = 196, or they use the square's side 7*sqrt(2) as the rectangle's height. The rectangle's height is the square's diagonal, not its side, because J and L are opposite vertices of the square.

questions.question:
In the figure above, WXYZ is a rectangle and T is a point on side XY.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Column A: The area of triangular region WTZ
Column B: The sum of the areas of triangular regions WXT and TYZ
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="40" y="50" width="230" height="130"/><line x1="40" y1="180" x2="150" y2="50"/><line x1="150" y1="50" x2="270" y2="180"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="26" y="196">W</text><text x="28" y="44">X</text><text x="272" y="44">Y</text><text x="272" y="196">Z</text><text x="146" y="42">T</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Let the rectangle have base WZ = b and height XW = h. Triangle WTZ has base WZ = b, and its apex T sits on the opposite side, so its height is the full h. Its area is (1/2)(b)(h), exactly half the rectangle's area bh. The two corner triangles WXT and TYZ together make up whatever is left of the rectangle, which is the other half. So the two quantities are equal, wherever T sits on XY.
questions.trap: Students try to compute the corner triangles separately, notice that T is not marked as a midpoint, and choose 'cannot be determined'. Sliding T along XY changes the two corner triangles individually but never changes their total, because the big triangle always claims exactly half the rectangle.

questions.question:
In the figure above, line BD is parallel to line AE, point B lies on segment AC, and point D lies on segment CE. Point F lies below line AE. The distance from C to line BD, marked y, equals the distance from F to line AE, marked x.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Column A: The area of triangular region ACE
Column B: The area of triangular region BDF
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="320" height="190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="35,120 160,20 285,120"/><line x1="110" y1="60" x2="210" y2="60"/><line x1="110" y1="60" x2="160" y2="160"/><line x1="210" y1="60" x2="160" y2="160"/><line x1="160" y1="20" x2="160" y2="60" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="160" y1="120" x2="160" y2="160" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><polyline points="160,50 170,50 170,60"/><polyline points="160,130 170,130 170,120"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="22" y="134">A</text><text x="96" y="56">B</text><text x="155" y="14">C</text><text x="214" y="56">D</text><text x="290" y="134">E</text><text x="152" y="178">F</text><text x="166" y="42">y</text><text x="150" y="133">x</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Let d be the distance between the two parallel lines BD and AE. The height of triangle ACE, measured from C down to base AE, is y + d. The height of triangle BDF, measured from F up to base BD, is x + d. Since x = y, those two heights are equal, so the areas are decided entirely by the bases. Now BD is a segment cut across triangle ACE parallel to AE with B on AC and D on CE, so BD is strictly shorter than AE. A larger base with the same height gives a larger area, so triangle ACE is greater.
questions.trap: Students compare only x with y, see that they are equal, and choose 'equal'. The two triangles do share a common height, but their bases differ: BD is a shortened copy of AE produced by the parallel cut, so equal heights leave ACE strictly bigger.

questions.question:
Line segment AD has length 40. Point B lies on AD, and segment BD has length 22. Point C also lies on AD, and segment BC has length 5.
Column A: The length of AC
Column B: The length of AB
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Since B is on AD with BD = 22, we get AB = 40 - 22 = 18, so Column B is fixed at 18. But C is only pinned down as a point of AD that is 5 units from B, and there are two such points: one 5 units toward A, giving AC = 13, and one 5 units toward D, giving AC = 23. Both lie within the segment, since 13 and 23 are both between 0 and 40. So Column A can be less than 18 or greater than 18, and the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Students place C automatically on the far side of B, compute AC = 23, and answer that Column A is greater. Saying that C is on the segment and 5 units from B leaves two legitimate positions, and the two give opposite comparisons.

questions.question: What is the ratio of the area of a square region with diagonal 6 to the area of a square region with diagonal 15? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explanation: A square with diagonal d has side d/sqrt(2), so its area is d^2/2. The first square has area 36/2 = 18 and the second has area 225/2 = 112.5. The ratio is 18/112.5 = 4/25. More directly, area scales as the square of any single length measurement, so the ratio of areas is (6/15)^2 = (2/5)^2 = 4/25.
questions.trap: Students report 6/15 = 2/5, giving the ratio of the diagonals rather than the ratio of the areas. Areas of similar figures scale as the square of the length ratio, so the 2/5 must be squared.

questions.question: A boat builder is cutting two sails, each in the shape of a right triangle whose legs are a vertical edge and a horizontal edge. Sail A has a vertical edge of length 24 feet and a hypotenuse of length 26 feet. Sail B has a vertical edge of length 20 feet and a hypotenuse of length 20.5 feet. How many square feet greater is the area of sail A than the area of sail B?
questions.explanation: For sail A the horizontal edge is sqrt(26^2 - 24^2) = sqrt(676 - 576) = sqrt(100) = 10, so its area is (1/2)(24)(10) = 120 square feet. For sail B the horizontal edge is sqrt(20.5^2 - 20^2) = sqrt(420.25 - 400) = sqrt(20.25) = 4.5, so its area is (1/2)(20)(4.5) = 45 square feet. The difference is 120 - 45 = 75 square feet.
questions.trap: Students take the hypotenuse as the second leg and compute areas of (1/2)(24)(26) = 312 and (1/2)(20)(20.5) = 205, reporting 107. In a right triangle only the two legs multiply to twice the area; the hypotenuse must first be converted into the missing leg by the Pythagorean theorem.

questions.question:
A plank 26 feet long rests horizontally on a support placed at the plank's midpoint, and the top of the support is 5 feet above level ground, as shown above. The plank is then tilted about the support, which stays at the plank's midpoint, until the left end of the plank just touches the ground. How many feet above the ground is the right end of the plank at that moment?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><line x1="15" y1="195" x2="305" y2="195"/><line x1="20" y1="195" x2="221" y2="128"/><polygon points="125,195 155,195 140,155"/><line x1="140" y1="155" x2="190" y2="155" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="190" y1="155" x2="190" y2="195" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="221" y1="128" x2="221" y2="195" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><polyline points="211,195 211,185 221,185"/></g><circle cx="140" cy="155" r="4" fill="#1f2937"/><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="70" y="159">26 ft</text><text x="152" y="177">5 ft</text><text x="229" y="165">?</text><text x="246" y="212">Ground</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: The support touches the plank at its midpoint, so each half of the plank is 13 feet long. Look at the left half: it runs from the support, 5 feet above the ground, down to the ground, so it is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with vertical leg 5 and hypotenuse 13 (a 5-12-13 triangle). The right half is the same 13-foot length tilted by the same angle in the opposite direction, so its far end rises 5 feet above the support. The support is already 5 feet up, so the right end is 5 + 5 = 10 feet above the ground.
questions.trap: Students answer 5, reading off only the height gained above the support, or they answer 13 by treating the half-plank as vertical. The two halves are mirror images about the support, so the right end climbs as far above the support as the left end dropped below it, and the support's own 5 feet must be added on.

questions.question:
A surveyor measures the distance from a marker M to post P as 18 metres and the distance from M to post Q as 11 metres. The three points are not in a straight line. Which of the following could be the distance, in metres, between P and Q?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: Because M, P and Q form a genuine triangle, the side PQ must be greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum: 18 - 11 = 7 and 18 + 11 = 29, so 7 < PQ < 29. Of the choices, 12, 20 and 28 lie strictly inside that range. 5 is too small, 7 is the excluded lower bound, and 31 exceeds the upper bound.
questions.trap: Students admit 7, forgetting that a distance of exactly 7 would put all three points on one line, which the problem rules out. The two bounds 7 and 29 are the collinear cases and are never attainable for a real triangle.

questions.question:
A cycling route runs in a straight line from a trailhead to a lookout 62.5 kilometres away. A water station stands on the route 47.2 kilometres from the trailhead, and a ranger is always within 0.8 kilometre of the water station, measured along the route. A cyclist's bicycle broke down on the route at a point less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout. Which of the following could be the distance, in kilometres, along the route between the bicycle and the ranger?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: Measure everything from the trailhead. The bicycle sits strictly between 62.5 - 0.6 = 61.9 and 62.5, since 'less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout' excludes both endpoints. The ranger sits somewhere from 47.2 - 0.8 = 46.4 to 47.2 + 0.8 = 48.0. The gap between them is smallest when the bicycle is as far back as possible and the ranger as far forward as possible: 61.9 - 48.0 = 13.9. It is largest when the bicycle is as far forward as possible and the ranger as far back as possible: 62.5 - 46.4 = 16.1. Both extremes come from the bicycle's excluded endpoints, so the distance runs strictly between 13.9 and 16.1. Only 14.0, 14.8 and 15.6 qualify.
questions.trap: Students take 16.1 because it looks like the stated maximum. Reaching 16.1 would require the bicycle to be exactly at the lookout, which the phrase 'less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout' forbids, so the top of the range is open. Others compute the centre gap 62.5 - 47.2 = 15.3 and spread it only by 0.8, missing the 0.6 from the bicycle's own uncertainty.
